# Interview Launchpad

Thanks for buying this. Here is everything you need to know, in about 60 seconds of reading.

---

## Start here

1. **Unzip this folder** somewhere permanent — your Documents folder, not your Downloads, and **not inside the zip preview window**.
2. **Double-click `index.html`.** It opens in your browser. That is the whole installation.
3. Work through the four setup steps: resume → target role and timeline → diagnostic → generate.

No account. No login. No internet needed. Nothing to install.

> **Important:** open `index.html` from a real folder on your disk. If you open it directly from inside the zip viewer, your browser blocks local storage and **your progress will not save** — the app will warn you in an orange banner if this happens.

---

## Your resume never leaves your laptop

There is no server. There is no account. There is no telemetry, no analytics, and nothing is uploaded.

You do not have to take my word for it: **turn off your Wi-Fi and use the whole thing.** It works identically. That is the proof.

Your resume is read by JavaScript running in your own browser, matched against a keyword list, and then discarded when you close the tab. The only thing kept is your plan and your ticked progress, in your browser's local storage.

**Resume formats:** `.txt`, `.md` and `.docx` are read directly. **PDFs cannot be parsed reliably in a browser** — open your PDF, press Ctrl+A then Ctrl+C, and paste it into the text box instead. That works perfectly, and it is why the paste box exists.

You can also skip the resume step entirely. It only affects which topics get compressed to a quick verify.

---

## How the plan works

**It braids.** Every week mixes two or three subjects plus DSA plus a project step — never one subject for a month. This is deliberate: study a topic in month one and leave it alone, and it is cold by the time you interview. Interleaved practice is harder week to week and remembered far better, which is the entire point.

**It adapts, in three ways:**
- **Your diagnostic** — a section under 50% gets extra hours and its topics are marked *focus area*.
- **Your resume** — a skill you can already prove is compressed to a *verify* pass instead of taught from scratch.
- **Your real hours** — this is the part most plans lie about.

**It tells you what it cut.** If your timeline and weekly hours cannot fit the full curriculum, the Progress tab lists exactly which topics did not make it, in priority order. Most plans quietly pretend everything fits and let you feel like the failure when it does not. Your hours are a hard constraint, and you deserve to see the consequence.

---

## Back up your progress

Your progress lives in this browser only. It does **not** sync between devices, and clearing your browser data erases it.

**Progress → Export progress file** writes a small `.json` you can keep or move to another machine (**Import** restores it). Do this before you switch laptops, clear history, or if the chip at the top ever says *not saved*.

Watch that chip. Green *saved* means it is working. That is the only status that matters.

---

## Honest expectations

- **This will not get you a job.** It decides what you study and keeps you honest about the hours. The work is still yours.
- **The explanations are concise on purpose.** Every topic links to primary documentation — read that, not a summary of it.
- **~50 well-understood DSA problems beat 150 half-remembered ones**, but be aware that strong candidates often arrive with more. If you find extra hours, DSA is where the first one should go.
- **Do not use this during a live interview.** Interview processes in 2026 increasingly detect assistance, and getting caught is worse than being unprepared.

---

## Practical tips from the first users

- **Tick steps as you finish them, not at the end of the week.** The progress bar only motivates if it is honest.
- **Take the week quiz cold** — no notes. A quiz you pass by looking things up has taught you nothing about what you will recall under pressure.
- **Do the project step every single week.** Interviewers ask about your project far more than your syllabus. One deployed thing you can explain beats four half-built repos.
- **Run your code.** The most common reason a correct approach fails an interview is that it was never executed. Type it, run it, then say you are done.
- **If a week collapses, do not restart the plan.** Mark it in progress, carry on, and let the plan absorb it. Guilt-driven restarts are how people quit in week 3.
